headline: Massachusetts auditor calls liquor-license system a barrier to restaurant growth
dek: A new report says population-based quotas have created shortages in 64 municipalities, left thousands of permits unused elsewhere and pushed some license prices into six figures.
body: A Massachusetts State Auditor’s Office report is calling for a major rewrite of the way cities and towns obtain liquor licenses, arguing that a population-based quota created in 1933 now restricts restaurant growth and makes access depend too heavily on money and political connections. The [auditor’s Oct. 13 announcement](https://www.mass.gov/news/state-auditors-report-identifies-barriers-in-massachusetts-liquor-license-process) says the review examined municipal licensing data, surveyed 260 officials and business owners, and interviewed license holders, municipal officials, legislators and industry participants.

The report, titled [License to Pour: Access and Equity in Massachusetts Liquor Licensing](https://www.mass.gov/report/license-to-pour-access-equity-in-massachusetts-liquor-licensing), describes a system with shortages in some communities and unused capacity in others. The Boston Globe reported that the analysis found 64 of the state’s 351 municipalities had too few licenses under the current arrangement, while 238 had not used their full allotments. That left 3,466 alcohol permits unused based on fiscal 2024 data, according to the Globe’s account of the report.

For businesses, the difference can be measured in the price of entry. The auditor’s office said owners reported paying $600,000 for a license in Boston, $175,000 in Somerville and $100,000 in Beverly, while a business in Cambridge—one of the municipalities with local control—reported an acquisition cost of $2,500. Boston 25 News independently described the same contrast and reported that the office believes the system favors wealthier communities and applicants with greater financial resources.

The state’s framework generally links the number of on-premises licenses available in a municipality to population. A business that wants to open a restaurant, bar, hotel or club must work through local licensing authorities and, for retail licenses, the state Alcoholic Beverages Control Commission. The commission’s [application guidance](https://www.mass.gov/apply-for-an-alcoholic-beverages-license-abcc) says retail applications begin with the municipality and then proceed through state review. In quota communities, an owner who cannot obtain a new license may instead have to buy one from an existing holder on a private secondary market.

The audit also identifies a built-in comparison inside Massachusetts. Twenty-six municipalities were allowed to keep local control after a limited period between 1978 and 1984, according to the auditor’s office and Globe reporting. That exception created what the report describes as a two-tier system: some communities can respond more directly to local demand, while others must seek additional licenses through the Legislature. The Globe reported that about 20 home-rule petitions seeking more licenses were filed during the current legislative session.

The economic stakes in the report are estimates, not guaranteed results. Comparing Massachusetts with neighboring states, the auditor’s office said matching the regional average for full-service restaurants could mean about 490 additional restaurants, 9,500 jobs, $311 million in annual wages and $56 million in yearly state and local meals-tax revenue. Those figures describe a potential opportunity under a different licensing environment; they do not mean the state would automatically create those businesses or collect that money if the quota changed.

The office recommends eliminating the state-imposed population quota for on-premises licenses, expanding local control, addressing the wealth and information barriers in the resale market, and creating a statewide public licensing-data platform. Auditor Diana DiZoglio said the system should remain compatible with responsible alcohol regulation while giving local businesses a fairer path to compete. The recommendations do not change the law, and the report does not itself grant any new licenses.

The next step is political rather than administrative. Any statewide change would require action by the Legislature, and local control has been debated without reaching a final overhaul. The report gives lawmakers a new set of statewide measurements and community examples, while restaurant owners still face the existing application, review and resale rules. For cities such as Boston, Somerville and Beverly, the immediate question is whether lawmakers will act on the evidence of high prices; for Cambridge and the other local-control communities, the question is whether their experience will be used as a model for broader reform.
location: Massachusetts, with examples from Boston, Somerville, Beverly and Cambridge
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Massachusetts liquor-license report finds equity and restaurant-growth barriers
seoDescription: A Massachusetts auditor’s report says population-based liquor-license quotas create shortages, unused permits and high resale prices.
